'''Richard Allan Andersen''' (November 16, 1942 – June 16, 2019)<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|title=Richard A. Andersen|url=https://senate.universityofcalifornia.edu/in-memoriam/files/richard-andersen.html|access-date=2021-05-19|website=senate.universityofcalifornia.edu}}</ref> was a professor of chemistry at the [[University of California, Berkeley]], and faculty senior scientist at the chemical sciences division of [[Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory]].<ref name=":1">{{Cite web|title=In Memoriam: Richard Andersen {{!}} College of Chemistry|url=https://chemistry.berkeley.edu/news/memoriam-richard-andersen|access-date=2021-05-19|website=chemistry.berkeley.edu}}</ref>

== Early life and career ==
Born in [[Oklahoma]] in 1942, Richard Allan Andersen was raised and educated in the small town of [[Yankton, South Dakota|Yankton]], [[South Dakota]].<ref name=":2">{{Cite journal|last1=Arnold|first1=John|last2=Tilley|first2=T. Don|date=2018-10-26|title=An enigmatic trailblazer on the frontier of discovery: Richard A. Andersen|url=https://pubs.rsc.org/en/content/articlelanding/2018/cc/c8cc90464b|journal=Chemical Communications|language=en|volume=54|issue=86|pages=12131–12132|doi=10.1039/C8CC90464B|pmid=30324202 |issn=1364-548X|url-access=subscription}}</ref> He obtained his bachelor's degree in 1965 from the [[University of South Dakota]].<ref name=":1" /> Andersen pursued graduate studies at the [[University of Wyoming]], working under the supervision of Professor [[Geoffrey E. Coates|Geoffrey Coates]].<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":2" /> Andersen was Coates' last student.<ref name=":2" /> In 1973, Andersen earned his Ph.D. with studies on several fundamental organometallic and alkoxide compounds of beryllium.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Andersen|first1=R. A.|last2=Bell|first2=N. A.|last3=Coates|first3=G. E.|date=1972|title=t-Butoxyberyllium halides and related compounds: the series X2Be3(OBut)4|url=http://xlink.rsc.org/?DOI=dt9720000577|journal=Journal of the Chemical Society, Dalton Transactions|language=en|issue=4|pages=577–582|doi=10.1039/dt9720000577|issn=0300-9246|url-access=subscription}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Andersen|first1=R. A.|last2=Coates|first2=G. E.|date=1972-01-01|title=Some sterically hindered beryllium alkoxides and their derivatives; monomeric beryllium 2,6-di-t-butylphenoxide|url=https://pubs.rsc.org/en/content/articlelanding/1972/dt/dt9720002153|journal=Journal of the Chemical Society, Dalton Transactions|language=en|issue=19|pages=2153–2155|doi=10.1039/DT9720002153|issn=1364-5447|url-access=subscription}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Andersen|first1=Richard A.|last2=Coates|first2=Geoffrey E.|date=1974-01-01|title=Reactions of beryllium alkyls with carbonyl and azomethine groups: addition, reduction, complex formation, and ortho-metallation|url=https://pubs.rsc.org/en/content/articlelanding/1974/dt/dt9740001171|journal=Journal of the Chemical Society, Dalton Transactions|language=en|issue=11|pages=1171–1180|doi=10.1039/DT9740001171|issn=1364-5447|url-access=subscription}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Andersen|first1=Richard A.|last2=Coates|first2=Geoffrey E.|date=1974|title=Alkoxyberyllium tetrahydroborates: t-butoxyberyllium pentane-2,4-dionate and complexes of t-butoxyberyllium oxide|url=http://dx.doi.org/10.1039/dt9740001440|journal=Journal of the Chemical Society, Dalton Transactions|issue=13|pages=1440|doi=10.1039/dt9740001440|issn=0300-9246|url-access=subscription}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Andersen|first1=Richard A.|last2=Coates|first2=Geoffrey E.|date=1974-01-01|title=Alkali-metal alkylberyllium alkoxides|url=https://pubs.rsc.org/en/content/articlelanding/1974/dt/dt9740001729|journal=Journal of the Chemical Society, Dalton Transactions|language=en|issue=16|pages=1729–1736|doi=10.1039/DT9740001729|issn=1364-5447|url-access=subscription}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Andersen|first1=Richard A.|last2=Coates|first2=Geoffrey E.|date=1975-01-01|title=Dimeric bis(nonafluoro-t-butoxy)beryllium and some of its co-ordinatio complexes|url=https://pubs.rsc.org/en/content/articlelanding/1975/dt/dt9750001244|journal=Journal of the Chemical Society, Dalton Transactions|language=en|issue=12|pages=1244–1245|doi=10.1039/DT9750001244|issn=1364-5447|url-access=subscription}}</ref>

Andersen then spent a year as postdoctoral researcher at the Oslo Centre for Industrial Research.<ref name=":3">{{Cite journal|last=Carmona|first=Ernesto|date=2019-12-09|title=Richard Allan Andersen (November 16, 1942–June 16, 2019): A Tribute|journal=Organometallics|volume=38|issue=23|pages=4523–4532|doi=10.1021/acs.organomet.9b00756|issn=0276-7333|doi-access=free}}</ref> On the day it was announced that [[Geoffrey Wilkinson]] and [[Ernst Otto Fischer|Ernst O. Fisher]] would share the 1973 [[Nobel Prize in Chemistry]], Andersen received an offer to conduct his postdoctoral research in Wilkinson's laboratory at [[Imperial College London]].<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":2" /> Andersen took up this post a few months later, in 1974.<ref name=":3" /> In June 1976 he joined the faculty at the University of California, Berkeley's department of chemistry.<ref name=":0" /> He remained a professor in the department until his death in 2019.<ref name=":0" />

Andersen was also active in teaching throughout his career, and was well-known for teaching from the primary inorganic chemistry literature,<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Stewart|first1=Joanne L.|last2=Bentley|first2=Anne K.|last3=Johnson|first3=Adam R.|last4=Nataro|first4=Chip|last5=Reisner|first5=Barbara A.|last6=Watson|first6=Lori A.|date=2018-10-09|title=Teaching from the primary inorganic literature: lessons from Richard Andersen|url=https://pubs.rsc.org/en/content/articlelanding/2018/dt/c8dt02669f|journal=Dalton Transactions|language=en|volume=47|issue=39|pages=13755–13760|doi=10.1039/C8DT02669F|pmid=30234873 |issn=1477-9234|url-access=subscription}}</ref> as well as his hands-on approach to teaching undergraduate laboratory courses.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":1" />

== Research ==
Andersen began his independent research career at UC Berkeley in 1976. Initially his research focused on ligand substitution patterns in quadruply-bonded Mo<sub>2</sub> complexes.<ref name=":2" /> He also studied actinide coordination complexes bearing the [[Metal bis(trimethylsilyl)amides|sterically bulky amido ligand –N(SiMe<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>]], including the uranium(III) compound U[N(SiMe<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>]<sub>3,</sub><ref name=":2" /><ref>{{Cite journal|last=Andersen|first=Richard A.|date=1979-06-01|title=Tris((hexamethyldisilyl)amido)uranium(III): preparation and coordination chemistry|url=https://doi.org/10.1021/ic50196a021|journal=Inorganic Chemistry|volume=18|issue=6|pages=1507–1509|doi=10.1021/ic50196a021|issn=0020-1669|url-access=subscription}}</ref> which was later found to have pyramidal geometry.<ref>{{Cite journal|date=1998-03-30|title=Trivalent uranium chemistry: molecular structure of [(Me3Si)2N]3U|url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0277538797002441|journal=Polyhedron|language=en|volume=17|issue=5–6|pages=953–958|doi=10.1016/S0277-5387(97)00244-1|issn=0277-5387|last1=Stewart |first1=Joanne L. |last2=Andersen |first2=Richard A. |url-access=subscription}}</ref>

== Awards and honors ==

Andersen was awarded many Visiting Professorships around the world, including appointments in Sevilla, Lyon, Montpellier, New South Wales, and Zurich.<ref name=":2" /> He was also an [[Alexander von Humboldt Professorship|Alexander von Humboldt Professor]] in various locations in Germany (1994).<ref name=":2" /><ref name=":4">{{Cite web|title=Richard A. Andersen {{!}} College of Chemistry|url=https://chemistry.berkeley.edu/faculty/chem/andersen|access-date=2021-05-19|website=chemistry.berkeley.edu}}</ref> Andersen was also a member of the [[Royal Society of Chemistry|Royal Chemical Society]], [[American Chemical Society]], and [[Sigma Xi Scientific Research Society|Sigma Xi]].<ref name=":4" />
